question: Tell me about a time you launched an AI-powered product or feature. What was your process from ideation through launch, and what did you learn?
strong:
At my last company I led the launch of an AI assistant that helped customer-success reps summarize account health and draft outreach. We started with discovery: ride-alongs, ticket analysis, and a few low-fidelity prompts in a shared notebook to see what GPT-4 could do out of the box. 

Architecturally, we chose a RAG approach over fine-tuning because content changed weekly and we needed governance. I stood up a pipeline that chunked and embedded CRM notes, QBR decks, and product telemetry docs into a vector store (we used pgvector for cost and ops simplicity). The app server handled retrieval, prompt construction with tools metadata, and a lightweight guardrail layer for PII redaction.

We iterated with an evaluation harness: synthetic cases plus real, anonymized tickets, scored along factuality, coverage, and style, with regression tests on each prompt or model change. For launch, we built feature flags, latency SLOs, and a fallback to template-based summaries. 

We learned that grounding data quality mattered more than model choice, and that exposing retrieval snippets to users dramatically increased trust and reduced "hallucination" complaints.
borderline:
I helped launch an AI-based knowledge assistant for our internal support team. The goal was to let agents query past tickets and documentation in natural language. We started with stakeholder interviews and a quick prototype using OpenAI’s API and our existing knowledge base. 

We debated between fine-tuning and retrieval and ended up using a retrieval-style approach because our content changed often and we wanted to avoid frequent re-training. I set up an ingestion job that indexed articles into a vector database and built a simple backend that took a user question, retrieved top documents, and constructed a prompt for the LLM. 

We did informal evaluation with a pilot group and tracked subjective quality and resolution time. From there, we refined prompts and improved how we chunked documents. For production, I worked with engineering to add logging, some basic redaction, and rate limiting. 

What I learned is that aligning with real workflows and maintaining the data pipeline are just as important as the model choice, and that we needed more systematic evaluation earlier.
weak:
I was involved in adding an AI feature to our product that helped users get automated answers from our help center. My role was mostly on the product side, but I also worked a bit with the engineers. 

We started by identifying common support questions and then connected our help articles to an LLM using a third-party tool. The main idea was that the model could read our FAQs and then respond in a friendly tone. I helped write the initial prompts and sample dialogues and decided what kind of answers we wanted, like brief vs. detailed. 

The engineers handled the integration and infrastructure, and we tested it with a beta group to see if the answers felt accurate and on-brand. We mostly iterated by tweaking the prompt and which articles were included. 

I learned that clear instructions in the prompt matter a lot, and that you have to watch out for the AI making things up, but I didn’t go deep into the technical architecture or training side.
